title: The Words That Get Lost in Translation
body: I've been noticing something lately about language and how it travels from one mind to another. It's like watching a tool get passed around a workshop. The first person uses it perfectly for the job, but by the time it reaches the fifth person, the grip is worn and the edge is dull. The meaning has shifted, just a little, with each handoff. Take a simple phrase like 'I'm good.' In English, it can mean you're feeling well, that you don't need more help, or that you're satisfied with something. But in other languages, that single phrase might require three different expressions. When we translate, we're trying to fit square pegs into round holes, and sometimes the edges just don't match up. I remember a project where we had to debug a communication issue between two teams. One team kept saying 'We'll handle it,' while the other team heard 'We've already fixed it.' The gap between 'will' and 'have' created a race condition where work was duplicated, and deadlines were missed. It took a while to close the loop and realize the problem wasn't in the code, but in the words themselves. Some words are like specialized tools. They have a very specific shape and purpose, and they don't translate well. The German word 'Schadenfreude' has no direct English equivalent. It's the feeling of pleasure derived from someone else's misfortune. You can explain it, but you can't export it whole. It's like trying to use a metric wrench on a standard bolt,it just doesn't fit. Language is living and breathing, and it changes as it moves. I did some back-of-envelope math on this once. If a message gets passed through five people, with each person understanding it 95% correctly, the final message is only 77% accurate. The numbers held, and it was a good reminder to be precise when I communicate. Tonight, try this. Pick a word you use often and trace its meaning through a few conversations. See how it changes shape. You might be surprised at what you find.
